content_voiceover: Let's cover ABO subgroups, a favorite board topic. Subgroups are weaker variants of A or B antigen expression caused by less efficient transferase enzymes. Note the ethnic variation: A2 is the most common subgroup among Caucasians, whereas in Taiwanese and Chinese populations, B3 is the most common ABO subgroup, found in roughly 1 in 900 group B individuals, followed by Ael. Serologically, B3 red cells react only weakly, about 1 to 2 plus, with anti-B reagent, and characteristically show a mixed field pattern, meaning some cells agglutinate while others in the same field do not. That mixed field appearance is a key recognition clue on boards for a subgroup rather than a true negative. Overall, ABO subgroups, including the Para Bombay types, account for roughly 0.079%, or about 1 in 1000, of blood donations based on the 2014 Taiwan subgroup database.
keypoints: B3 is the most common ABO subgroup in Chinese/Taiwanese (~1 in 900 group B); A2 is most common in Caucasians
B3 red cells show weak (1-2+), mixed-field reactions with anti-B — a classic subgroup clue
ABO subgroups overall make up about 0.079% (~1 in 1000) of donors
Weak subtypes like Ael can cause forward/reverse ABO typing discrepancies
